value.overview: The Striped Cuckoo (Tapera naevia) is a slender Neotropical cuckoo recognized by its strongly streaked upperparts, long tail, and distinctive whistled song. Unlike most North American cuckoos, it is an obligate brood parasite: it lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, especially species that build covered stick nests. It usually inhabits open or partly wooded landscapes rather than deep forest and is often easier to detect by voice than by sight.
value.classification: The Striped Cuckoo is the only species in the genus Tapera and belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae. It is one of the few obligate brood-parasitic cuckoos in the Americas.
value.identification: Adults are medium-sized, slim cuckoos with brown upperparts marked by conspicuous pale or whitish streaks, a pale eyebrow, buffy or whitish underparts, and a long, graduated tail with darker central feathers. The wings are rounded, and the bill is slightly curved. Its repeated, clear whistle is often the best way to locate it. When alarmed, it may raise or flash the small feathers near the wing bend, creating a noticeable pale-wing display.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a native lowland bird, recorded especially in open country, pastures, agricultural landscapes, scrub, second growth, woodland edges, and areas with scattered trees. It also occurs around mangroves and other semi-open habitats, generally from sea level into the foothills. Historical observations from southwestern Costa Rica found it locally common in disturbed second-growth areas, including around Sierpe.
value.migrationStatus: The Striped Cuckoo is generally considered a year-round resident, not a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs as a resident or regular local species, although numbers and detectability may vary seasonally and some individuals may make short local movements.
value.breeding: The Striped Cuckoo is an obligate brood parasite and does not build a nest, incubate its eggs, or raise its young. Females place an egg in the nest of another bird, commonly in the large covered or domed stick nests of spinetails, wrens, and related species. Confirmed Costa Rican host records include the Pale-breasted Spinetail, while local sources also report hosts among wrens and sparrow-like birds. Breeding records span much of the year, with activity documented from January through October.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including caterpillars, grasshoppers, beetles, and similar prey. It forages in low vegetation, shrubs, tangled growth, and along woodland edges, usually moving deliberately while searching among leaves and branches. It may also take small vertebrates or other foods opportunistically, but detailed information on the diet in Costa Rica is limited.
value.behavior: The Striped Cuckoo is secretive and often remains hidden in dense shrubs, vines, tall grass, or low woodland. It frequently gives its distinctive repeated whistle from a concealed perch. Individuals may sit quietly for long periods before moving through vegetation or flying between scattered trees. Females inspect potential host nests, and the cuckoo chick is dependent on the foster parents after hatching; in some cases the young cuckoo eliminates competing host nestlings.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species is widespread and has no reliable evidence of a major worldwide decline.
